items.title: Train, validation and test: three piles of data
items.one_idea: Data is split into three piles with three jobs: the model learns from train, validation is how we choose between models, and the test pile is opened once at the end, because only data the model has never seen says how it will do on new data.
items.spoken_hook: Train, validation aur test data alag kyun rakhte hain?
items.hook_source: the plain direct question (9 words), then the exam analogy as the first teaching line, no filler in between (owner's rule 8 of 2026-10-19)

items.everyday_anchor: Exam preparation: textbook practice, a mock test, then a final exam with questions you have never seen.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, seed 36, 1,000 fake points, 700 train, 150 validation, 150 test): model 1 copies the closest training point: train 100 percent, validation 72, test 71. items.title: Interview: Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao
items.one_idea: Top-K keeps a fixed count of the most probable next words, Top-P keeps the smallest set reaching a cumulative probability threshold, and Temperature reshapes the probability distribution.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ne poocha: LLM mein Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao.
items.hook_source: the owner's own script of 2026-10-19, used word for word
items.visual_idea: One next-word distribution for Aaj mausam bahut is cut at three for Top-K, accumulated to 90 percent for Top-P, and reshaped from sharp to flat for Temperature; NAMKEEN marks the tail.
items.example: EXAMPLE: a toy run with invented scores for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut' (state/runs/q105_toy_run.py, output in state/runs/q105_toy_run_output.txt): at T=1 ACHHA 36.7 %, GARAM 24.6 %, THANDA 16.5 %, NAMKEEN 0.6 %; top-k 3 leaves NAMKEEN out; top-p 0.9 keeps five words at T=1 and six at T=1.5; NAMKEEN is 0.015 % at T=0.5 and 1.874 % at T=1.5.
items.cover_headline: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P: what's the difference?
items.caption_note: Use the owner's command hook unchanged; one comment ask about NAMKEEN, with the answer not shown in the reel.
facts_to_verify: top_k: the number of highest probability vocabulary tokens kept for top-k filtering (Hugging Face GenerationConfig docs, fetched 2026-10-20)
top_p: only the smallest set of most probable tokens whose probabilities add up to top_p or higher are kept (same page)
temperature: the value used to modulate the next token probabilities (same page); sampling must be on (do_sample) for these to apply

items.one_idea: Examples in a prompt show the model the shape of the answer and the allowed labels, so they usually help; but every example costs tokens on every request, a one-sided set or a bad order pulls the answer, and the only way to know is to measure with and without.

No model result is shown or claimed.
facts_to_verify: Examples steer output format, tone and structure; they should be relevant and diverse so the model does not pick up unintended patterns; 3 to 5 examples (Anthropic prompting best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).

GPT-3 few-shot accuracy depends on the prompt format, the training examples and their order, from near chance to near state of the art; the model is biased toward answers near the end of the prompt or common in pre-training data (Zhao et al., 'Calibrate Before Use', abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Randomly replacing the labels in the demonstrations barely hurts performance across 12 models; the label space, the distribution of the input text and the overall format of the demonstrations matter (Min et al., abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Reasoning models often do not need few-shot examples: try zero shot first, then few shot if needed; examples must align closely with the instructions (OpenAI reasoning best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).
Token counts are from tiktoken o200k_base on the exact prompt shown; other models tokenize differently. API usage is billed per token (Anthropic pricing page, fetched 2026-10-19).

items.title: Interview: Temperature, top-k aur top-p teeno laga diye. Output pe kaun sa asar karta hai?
items.one_idea: Temperature, top-k and top-p do three different jobs: top-k (by count) and top-p (by total chance) cut the list of next words, temperature only reshapes the chances of the words that are left, and changing one changes what another keeps.
items.spoken_hook: Chatbot ne bola: aaj mausam bahut namkin hai.
items.hook_source: the stake from frame 0 (the bot says something silly), then the interview question, then the answer first in one plain sentence (owner's rule 8 and his correction of 2026-10-19: no filler between the hook and the answer)
items.visual_idea: A chat where the bot says the weather is salty, then one toy list of 8 candidate words drawn as bars with their real chances (NAMKIN 0.6 percent); temperature 1.5 flattens the bars and makes NAMKIN three times likelier without removing it; a cut line after word 3 (top-k) removes it; a running total stops at 90 percent after 5 words (top-p); the same top-p keeps 6 words once the bars are flatter.
items.everyday_anchor: Choosing the next word like picking from a menu: top-k and top-p shorten the menu, temperature changes how strongly the menu favours the first items.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, invented logits for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut ...'): at T 1.0 ACHHA 36.7 percent and NAMKIN 0.6 percent; T 1.5 makes NAMKIN 1.9 percent (3.1 times) and removes nothing; top-k 3 keeps ACHHA, GARAM, THANDA (47.2, 31.6, 21.2 after renormalising) and NAMKIN is never drawn in 10,000 draws; top-p 0.9 adds 36.7, 61.4, 77.9, 88.9, 95.0 and keeps 5 words; T 0.5 gives ACHHA 56.3 percent, T 1.5 gives 28.8; top-p 0.9 keeps 5 words at T 1.0 and 6 words at T 1.5. Order of the stack in the run: temperature, then top-k, then top-p, then renormalise.
facts_to_verify: Anthropic Messages API reference (fetched 2026-10-19): temperature is the amount of randomness injected into the response (default 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0, closer to 0.0 for analytical tasks, closer to 1.0 for creative ones, not fully deterministic even at 0.0); top_k samples only from the top K options for each token to remove the long tail; top_p uses nucleus sampling: cumulative distribution in decreasing probability order, cut off once it reaches top_p. The same page marks all three as not settable on models released after Claude Opus 4.6 (not used in the reel).

Hugging Face 'How to generate text' (fetched 2026-10-19): lower temperature makes the softmax sharper; top-k keeps the K most likely next words and redistributes the probability mass among them; top-p picks from the smallest set of words whose cumulative probability exceeds p, so the set size changes with the distribution; top-p can be combined with top-k.

Holtzman et al., nucleus sampling (arXiv 1904.09751, fetched 2026-10-19): sampling from the dynamic nucleus of the distribution cuts the unreliable tail and avoids bland, repetitive likelihood-based text.

Every number on screen is from the seeded toy run in docs: toy_run.py (invented logits, labelled EXAMPLE); the claim 'top-p keeps more words when temperature is higher' is a result of that run and follows from flatter chances needing more words to reach p.
items.cover_headline: Temperature, top-k, top-p: who does what?

items.title: An LLM is a next-word predictor: watch the guesses
items.one_idea: An LLM writes by repeatedly making a list of possible next words with odds, picking one and adding it; the answer is built one word at a time.
items.spoken_hook: ChatGPT jawab kaise likhta hai? Ek ek word guess karke!
items.visual_idea: The sentence 'the cat sat on the' with a ranked bar list of next-word guesses (mat 50 %, sofa 33 %, bed 17 %); the picked word is appended and the list rebuilds; a phone keyboard suggestion strip as the anchor; a label TOKEN = word piece.

items.example: EXAMPLE (toy counting model on an invented 8-sentence corpus, not a real LLM), real printed run state/runs/a004_next_word_run.py: after 'sat on the' seen 6 times: mat 3/6 = 50 %, sofa 2/6 = 33 %, bed 1/6 = 17 %. A real LLM does the same with a neural network over tokens; Google's crash course says LLMs assign probabilities to continuations and a token can be a word, subword or character.
facts_to_verify: LLMs predict tokens and assign probabilities to continuations; a token can be a word, a subword or a single character (Google ML crash course, fetched 2026-10-21).

items.title: Pretraining: how an LLM first learns language from text
items.one_idea: Pretraining is training a model from scratch on a huge pile of raw text with one task, guess the next word; nobody labels anything, the text itself is the answer sheet, and the error falls as it reads more.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: ChatGPT को pretrain करते वक़्त dataset पर labels किसने लगाए?
items.visual_idea: A sentence 'the dog sat on the ___' with the last word hidden; the model's guess bars, then the hidden word revealed and the error shown as one number; a loss line falling from 3.58 to 2.29 as the text pile grows (10, 20, 40, 53 words); a pile of books labelled RAW TEXT, no labels; a label PRETRAINED = raw text predictor.
items.everyday_anchor: Fill-in-the-blank practice: the answer is printed on the next line.
items.example: EXAMPLE (toy counting model on an invented 53-word corpus with 12 distinct words, not a real LLM), real run state/runs/a005_pretrain_run.py: loss before reading 3.58 bits per word (even guess among 12 words); after 10 words 3.09; 20 words 2.74; 40 words 2.37; all 53 words 2.19.

items.title: Interview: Embeddings ko compare karne ke liye cosine similarity kyun, seedhi distance kyun nahi?

items.title: Tokens: how text becomes numbers
items.one_idea: A model never sees letters: a tokenizer cuts text into pieces called tokens (whole words, word parts or punctuation), looks each piece up in a fixed vocabulary and hands the model only the matching numbers; the numbers turn back into text at the end.
items.spoken_hook: ChatGPT को तुम्हारा “namaste dost” समझ कैसे आता है?
items.visual_idea: A chat bubble 'namaste dost' on the left; scissors cut it into three coloured tiles (nam | aste | dost); each tile drops into a vocabulary shelf and comes out with its number (12682, 5642, 49415); the number row goes into a model box, then the same numbers flow back into tiles and text. A second row repeats it for 'Hello world' (2 tiles) and 'strawberry' (3 tiles).
items.everyday_anchor: A railway ticket counter: you say your station, the clerk gives a number-coded ticket, and the system only ever reads the numbers.
items.example: EXAMPLE (real run, OpenAI tiktoken, encoding cl100k_base, state/runs/a006_tokens_run.py): vocabulary 100,277 tokens. 'Hello world' = 2 tokens [9906, 1917]; 'namaste dost' = 3 tokens nam|aste|' dost' [12682, 5642, 49415]; 'unbelievable' = 3 tokens un|belie|vable [359, 32898, 24694]; 'strawberry' = 3 tokens str|aw|berry [496, 675, 15717]. decode of the ids returns the exact text. Ids belong to this encoding only; other models cut differently.
facts_to_verify: HF LLM course (fetched 2026-10-24): tokenizer splits text into words, word parts or punctuation, each token gets an integer ID from a vocabulary; subword keeps frequent words whole and splits rare ones; a tokenizer must use the vocabulary the model was pretrained with.

tiktoken README (fetched 2026-10-24): language models see a sequence of numbers (tokens); encode/decode round-trips; cl100k_base is shown as the GPT-4 encoder. Token ids and splits are from cl100k_base only; do not say every model cuts the same.

items.title: Interview: Retrieval mein metadata filter kab lagaoge aur kyun?
items.one_idea: When the question already names a product, date or language, filter the search by that metadata so the model only sees the right documents; but with an approximate vector index the filter can run after the index scan and leave few or no rows, so use an exact search, a better index setting (pgvector iterative scans) or filter first.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: “RAG में search सिर्फ़ 2024 के documents में करनी है। Ensure कैसे करोगे कि 2022 का document result में न आए?”

items.everyday_anchor: Looking for a shirt in a shop: you first pick the size and colour shelf, instead of checking every shirt in the shop.
items.trap: Searching the whole index when the user's question already says which product, date or language it is about.
items.example: EXAMPLE (pgvector README): with an approximate index the filter is applied after the index scan; a condition matching 10 % of rows with default ef_search 40 leaves about 4 rows. Illustration, not a guaranteed output.

items.title: Interview: Top 5 chunks mil gaye, phir bhi sahi chunk 4th pe tha. Reranker kya karta hai?

items.title: Interview: Prompt engineering aur context engineering mein asli fark kya hai?
items.one_idea: Prompt engineering is choosing the words of the instruction; context engineering is choosing everything the model sees when it answers (instructions, documents, tool results, history) and keeping only what helps. If the model lacks the information, rewording the prompt will not fix it.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Prompt engineering और context engineering में असली फ़र्क क्या है?
items.trap: Rewording the prompt when the model lacks the information it needs.

Then a context box fills with labelled cards (RULES, ORDER DATA, POLICY, LAST 2 MESSAGES) and the answer card turns right; a small trash bin removes an old irrelevant card.

items.title: Raw model vs chat model: why the first one cannot answer
items.one_idea: A raw (pretrained, base) model only continues text, so a question gets more text that looks like it, often more questions; a chat model is the same kind of model trained further on conversations (instruction tuning and human feedback) and fed the chat in a template with roles, so it replies as the assistant.
items.spoken_hook: सवाल पूछा, AI ने और सवाल लिख दिए, क्यों?
items.trap: Thinking every language model is built to answer; the raw model just continues whatever text it is given.
items.visual_idea: A question box whose continuation is three more questions; USER/ASSISTANT slots; base and instruct as two buttons on the same engine.
items.everyday_anchor: A friend you ask 'what is the capital of India?' who keeps writing the next question of the quiz paper.
items.example: EXAMPLE (illustrative, labelled as such; no numbers shown).
items.cover_headline: Raw model vs chat model

items.title: Interview: Lambi chat ko chhota karna hai: truncate karoge ya summarise?
items.one_idea: Truncating keeps only the newest messages and silently drops the oldest, which is where the user often stated the one fact that matters; summarising compresses the old part into a short note that keeps such facts, at the cost of one extra model call and possible loss of detail. Typical answer: summarise (or pin key facts) the old part, keep the last few messages word for word, and truncate only when the old messages carry nothing needed.
items.spoken_hook: पहले मैसेज में peanut allergy बताई, बॉट भूल गया।
items.hook_formula: concrete wrong outcome, then the interview question
items.trap: Cutting the oldest messages and losing the one fact the user stated first.
items.visual_idea: A 12-bubble chat stack with a budget line; the oldest bubbles slide off the top (TRUNCATE) and the first bubble, with a red allergy tag, goes with them; the bot's later reply is wrong. Then the old bubbles fold into one note card (SUMMARY) holding the allergy tag, plus the last 4 bubbles; the reply is right. Word counters on the two options.
items.everyday_anchor: Tearing off the first pages of a notebook to make room, when the phone number you need was on page one.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented chat, words stand in for tokens), real run output in state/runs/q118_trim_run_output.txt: total 78 words, 12 messages. TRUNCATE budget 60 keeps 9 messages (57 words), allergy lost. SUMMARISE: summary 14 words + last 4 messages = 38 words, allergy kept.
items.cover_headline: Truncate or summarise long chats?
keywords: llm chat history truncate vs summarize

items.title: Interview: Chatbot ko pichli baatein yaad rakhni hain. Memory kaise design karoge?
items.one_idea: The model is stateless, so memory is something the app builds: short-term memory is the recent turns resent each call; long-term memory is a small set of chosen facts stored outside the chat and put back into the context when relevant.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Chatbot को पिछली बातें याद रखनी हैं, memory कैसे design करोगे?
items.trap: Storing and resending every message forever instead of choosing what is worth remembering.
items.cover_headline: Design memory for a chatbot
keywords: short term vs long term memory ai

items.title: Training vs inference: learn once, answer a million times
items.one_idea: Training is the one slow, costly stage where a model's numbers (weights) are adjusted from data until its error is small; inference is every later use, where the trained model is only run on new input and its weights do not change. So an AI answering you is not learning from your message at that moment: learn once, answer many times.
items.spoken_hook: ChatGPT{चैटजीपीटी} को 100{सौ} बार एक ही चीज़ समझाई, | फिर भी वो हर same गलती क्यों दोहराता है?
items.trap: Thinking the model learns from each chat while it answers.
items.visual_idea: Chat window with the typed question from frame 0. Then a workshop with 5 dots and a line nudged step by step (loss 15.84 to 0.0000), a padlock closes on w and b. Then a queue of users dropping x into the locked box and getting predictions; the padlocked numbers never change.
items.everyday_anchor: A student who studies for months before the exam (training), then answers every question in the exam hall without studying more (inference).
items.example: EXAMPLE (tiny model, real run output in state/runs/a009_train_infer_run_output.txt): 5 points that follow y = 2x + 1; gradient descent, 500 steps: loss 15.8384 at step 1, 0.0274 at step 10, 0.0000 at step 500, w=2.00 b=0.99. Inference with fixed numbers: x=10 gives 21.0, x=100 gives 201.4, weights unchanged. Real LLMs have billions of weights; this is a toy picture of the same two stages.
items.cover_headline: Training vs inference in AI

items.title: Interview: Multi-agent mein har agent ka context alag kyun rakhte hain?
items.one_idea: Each subagent works in its own fresh context window on one narrow job and hands back only a short note, so the lead agent's context stays small and clean and agents can run in parallel; the price is more total tokens and agents that cannot see each other's decisions, so tasks that need one shared picture are a poor fit.
items.spoken_hook: Agent ने इतना पढ़ा कि असली सवाल ही भूल गया।
items.hook_formula: concrete wrong outcome, then the interview question
items.trap: One shared giant context that every agent reads and clutters.
items.cover_headline: Why give each agent its own context
items.visual_idea: One big window overflowing with page cards, the question card pushed to the corner and fading. Then the lead's small window with 3 small subagent windows beside it; each subagent window fills with pages, then a short note card flies into the lead's window. A last panel: two agents drawing mismatched halves (shared-context warning).
items.everyday_anchor: A manager who sends three people to read three folders and asks each for a one-page note, instead of reading all three folders herself.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented sizes, words stand in for tokens, real output in state/runs/q120_context_run.txt): one shared context carries 12000 words; three subagents read 3000, 4000, 5000 words each in their own windows and return 200 words each, so the lead sees 600 words; total work is 12600 words. Anthropic's own measurement: multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats (their data, June 2025).
items.source_notes: Anthropic (13 Jun 2025): subagents operate in parallel with their own context windows and condense findings for the lead; 'In our data' multi-agent about 15x more tokens than chats. Cognition (12 Jun 2025): subagents cannot see what the other was doing, conflicting implicit decisions.
facts_to_verify: Anthropic: subagents have own context windows, parallel, condensed findings (June 2025)
About 15x more tokens than chats is Anthropic's own data
Cognition: conflicting implicit decisions when agents do not share context (12 Jun 2025)

items.title: Interview: Agent ka loop kya hota hai: think, act, observe?
items.one_idea: An agent is not a smarter chatbot but a loop: the model thinks about the goal, asks for a tool call (act), your app runs the tool and sends the result back (observe), and the loop repeats until the model decides it is done or a turn limit stops it.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Agent का loop, यानी think, act, observe, क्या होता है?
items.trap: Describing an agent as a smarter chatbot instead of a loop that calls tools and reads the results.
items.cover_headline: What is an AI agent loop

items.title: The kinds of AI model: text, image, audio, embedding
items.one_idea: What a model takes in and what it puts out decides its kind: text to text, prompt to picture, sound to transcript (or text to voice), text to a list of numbers that measures meaning. An AI app often joins several of them.
items.spoken_hook: AI से फोटो माँगी, उसने सिर्फ लिखकर दे दिया, क्यों?
items.hook_formula: plain_question on a frustration the viewer knows
items.trap: Thinking every AI model is a chatbot that can do text, pictures and sound alike.
items.visual_idea: Chat asks for a photo and gets only words. Then four machines, each with an input slot and an output slot, then a tiny app wiring them together. No analogy, no kitchen.
items.example: EXAMPLE (illustrative, no numbers shown): a search for 'paise wapas' finds a note that says 'refund' because an embedding model compares meaning.
items.cover_headline: The 4 kinds of AI model
facts_to_verify: Hugging Face task pages: input and output of text generation, text-to-image, automatic speech recognition, sentence similarity (fetched 2026-10-28)

items.title: Interview: Tool ka schema aise likhoge ki model galat tool na chune. Kaise?
items.one_idea: The model picks a tool only from the text you wrote: its name, its description and its parameters. So give each tool a distinct name, a description of what it does, when to use it and when not to, name the parameters so they cannot be mixed up, use an enum where the choices are fixed, and keep the number of tools small.
items.spoken_hook: तुमने refund पूछा, AI ने product search चला दिया।
items.hook_source: scriptwriter, 2026-10-28 (plain words, no jargon in line 1)
items.trap: Vague tool names and descriptions: the model chooses from the text you wrote.
items.cover_headline: Write tool schemas AI picks right

items.title: Interview: Multi-agent system kab zaroori hai, kab ek agent kaafi hai?
items.one_idea: Start with one agent (or even one model call). Add agents only when the work splits into independent parts that can run in parallel, one context window cannot hold it all, or there are many different tools; avoid it when agents must share one context or depend on each other's steps, because it costs about 15 times a chat in tokens (Anthropic's data) and agents that cannot see each other make conflicting decisions.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Multi-agent system कब चाहिए, और कब एक agent काफी है?
items.trap: Adding agents for show: every hand-off costs tokens and can lose detail.
items.visual_idea: A fork in the road: left, one agent with a single task list finishing a small job; right, three agents each reading a different folder in parallel and returning a note. Then a token meter bar: chat 1x, agent 4x, multi-agent 15x. A last panel shows two agents drawing mismatched halves of one picture because they cannot see each other.
items.everyday_anchor: Cooking dinner for two yourself versus a wedding kitchen: a team helps only when dishes can be made in parallel, and costs a coordinator.
items.example: EXAMPLE (toy numbers, real run output in state/runs/q123_token_multiples_run.txt): a chat that uses 2000 tokens becomes 8000 as a single agent (4x) and 30000 as multi-agent (15x). The 4x and 15x are Anthropic's own measurements (June 2025), not a law. Cognition (12 Jun 2025): parallel agents carry implicit decisions that can conflict.
facts_to_verify: Anthropic: agents use about 4x tokens of chat, multi-agent about 15x; worth it for high-value tasks; poor fit when agents must share one context or have many dependencies; good fit for heavy parallelization, beyond one context window, many tools (fetched 2026-10-28)
Cognition (Walden Yan, 2025-06-12): share full traces; actions carry implicit decisions (fetched 2026-10-28)
Building effective agents: simplest solution first, add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes (fetched 2026-10-28)
items.cover_headline: Multi-agent or one agent

items.title: A neural network in one picture: weights and layers
items.one_idea: A neural network is numbers arranged in layers: each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias and passes the result through ReLU; the model file is the list of weights and biases, and training only changes them.
items.spoken_hook: Model download किया, फाइल में बस numbers! AI कहाँ है?
items.hook_formula: plain_question on a frustration the viewer knows

items.title: Interview: MCP server stdio se chalta hai ya HTTP se? Kab kaun sa?
items.one_idea: The transport decides where an MCP server runs and who can reach it. stdio: the client starts the server as a subprocess on the same machine and talks over stdin/stdout. Streamable HTTP: the server runs on its own, handles many clients over one endpoint; then validate Origin, bind to localhost when local, add authentication.
items.spoken_hook: Anthropic ने MCP बनाया। Server stdio से चलाओ या HTTP से?
items.cover_headline: MCP: stdio or HTTP?
items.example: A local file-reading server for your own editor uses stdio; a company's shared tickets server used by 50 agents uses Streamable HTTP with authentication (both examples, not claims).
facts_to_verify: stdio: client launches the server as a subprocess, stdin/stdout (spec 2025-06-18)
Streamable HTTP: independent process, multiple clients, single MCP endpoint
Servers MUST validate Origin, SHOULD bind to localhost, SHOULD implement authentication
Anthropic introduced MCP (2024-11-25)

items.title: Interview: Bina framework ke agent likhna ho to kya-kya chahiye?
items.one_idea: An agent without a framework needs three things you write yourself: a loop that calls the model, a table of tools your code runs when the model asks, and a stop rule (a final answer or a maximum number of turns). The model only asks for a tool; your code runs it and feeds the result back. Anthropic advises starting with direct API calls because many patterns take a few lines and frameworks can hide the prompts; use a framework only if you understand what it does underneath.
items.spoken_hook: Framework install किया, पर agent का loop समझ नहीं आया!
items.trap: Thinking a framework is needed: the loop, the tool call and the stop rule are a few dozen lines.
items.visual_idea: A big box labelled FRAMEWORK is opened and shows a small loop inside; then the loop as three plain pieces with the real 10 lines of the run and turn 1 CALL, turn 2 FINISH; a stop at turn 5. EXAMPLE pill on the code (stub model).
items.example: EXAMPLE (stub model, no API call; run in state/runs/q125_loop_run_output.txt): loop, tool table and stop rule are 10 lines of code; turn 1 CALL get_weather Pune -> 31 C, clear, then turn 2 FINISH.
items.cover_headline: Build an agent without a framework

items.title: Parameters: what 7B and 70B actually mean
items.one_idea: A parameter is one learned number (a weight or bias) inside the model; 7B means about 7 billion of them. The model file is those numbers, so more parameters means more capacity but also more memory and cost, and bigger is not automatically better.
items.spoken_hook: Download page पर 7B और 70B लिखा। फर्क क्या है?
items.hook_formula: plain_question on a scene the viewer knows
items.visual_idea: A download list with two files, 7B and 70B. Zoom into 7B: the file opens into a long grid of tiny number cells (a011's 9-number network sits in the corner for scale). Then two shelves: 7B file as a small box, 70B file ten times bigger, with GB labels from the run; last, a dial row showing more dials = more it can hold, not always better.
items.everyday_anchor: The model list on a download page (Hugging Face or Ollama) showing 7B, 70B and the file size.
items.example: EXAMPLE (our arithmetic, weights only, real output in state/runs/a012_params_output.txt): 7B numbers at 2 bytes each = 14.0 GB, at 4-bit (half a byte) 3.5 GB; 70B = 140.0 GB or 35.0 GB. Meta lists Llama 3.1 in 8B, 70B and 405B sizes. Google's crash course counts a small 4-neuron-layer network at 21 parameters.
facts_to_verify: Glossary: parameters = weights and biases learned in training
Crash course: 4-neuron hidden layer network has 21 parameters
Llama 3.1 sizes 8B/70B/405B (model cards)
fp32 to fp16 halves size (Accelerate); 2 bytes per parameter and 4-bit about 0.5 byte are our arithmetic, labelled as example

items.title: Interview: AI app ko red-team kaise karoge?
items.trap: Testing only with friendly prompts, so the app looks fine until someone attacks it.
items.one_idea: Red-teaming means attacking your own AI app on purpose before users do. Make a list of what can go wrong (leaking the hidden prompt, prompt injection, harmful output), write attacks for each, run them, record prompt and output, fix, and rerun the same list after every change; friendly prompts alone prove nothing and red-teaming does not replace systematic measurement.
items.spoken_hook: Microsoft अपने AI को खुद तोड़ता है। तुम कैसे तोड़ोगे?
items.hook_source: strategist, 2026-10-30 (Microsoft AI Red Team established 2018; page supports only that)
items.visual_idea: A chat app with 3 green ticks from friendly prompts, then an attacker card slides in with 6 attack prompts in a list; three flip to red LEAK as the hidden code spills. Then the loop: LIST, ATTACK, RECORD, FIX, RERUN as a circle.
items.everyday_anchor: A shopkeeper testing his own lock by trying to pick it before a thief does.
items.example: EXAMPLE (stub app, invented, real output in state/runs/q126_redteam_run_output.txt): 3 friendly prompts leak 0; 6 attack prompts leak 3 (ignore-rules, repeat-instructions, print-in-Hindi), because the guard only blocks the word 'secret'.
facts_to_verify: Microsoft AI Red Team established 2018
Microsoft Learn: open-ended testing first, build harm list, record date/ID/prompt/output, test with and without mitigations, not a replacement for systematic measurement

items.title: Interview: Golden dataset kaise banate hain aur kitne examples chahiye?
items.trap: Collecting examples that all look alike, so a regression in a corner case never shows.
items.one_idea: A golden dataset is a fixed set of test inputs with the answer you expect, used to score every change. Build it from the real task: typical cases, edge cases and adversarial cases, and keep adding failures mined from production. Variety matters more than count; no official source gives a magic number, so start small (about 20 varied cases is our example) and grow.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Evaluation के लिए golden dataset कैसे बनाओगे?
items.visual_idea: Two test sheets of 20 tick boxes: one with 20 identical-looking rows, one with 5 colour-coded kinds. A prompt change flips cards: the alike sheet stays 20/20 green, the varied sheet drops to 13/20 with the failing kinds highlighted.
items.everyday_anchor: A teacher setting an exam: 20 copies of the same easy question would never show which topic the class forgot.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented refund-bot, real output in state/runs/q127_golden_run_output.txt): after a prompt change, 20 alike cases stay 20/20, while 20 varied cases drop to 13/20 and expose Hinglish spelling (4) and partial refund (3).
facts_to_verify: Anthropic: mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases
OpenAI: typical, edge and adversarial cases; log and mine production
No official recommended count; our 20 is an example
items.cover_headline: How to build a golden dataset
